title: Recording technology and engineers who read scores
summary: Too many microphones and technology; an engineer should read the score, as Columbia engineers once did.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Are you much impressed by what's happened to the technology of recording since you started?
(Unintelligible) we got 20 mikes and all this. And we haven't got enough mikes for all the instruments you got. Paul Jeffries, my arranger, said what do you do for a symphony orchestra?

That's right. Because when London -- FFRR, when you first started, that was the first high frequency classical. And they'd record 100 classical with one mike up on the ceiling. It sounded great. So you think they've gotten overly involved with technology.
What about engineers? I've found during the year or so that I did A&R that an engineer could make an enormous difference.
An engineer should be able to read.
He should read the score and know what instruments to bring up at the time.
And they don't make them like that no more.
Yeah, I haven't been interested in --
(Unintelligible) with Columbia Records, and Tio was there, he could read (inaudible).
Was that Fred Plout, do you know, that --
Big guy, did a lot of classical dates, yeah.
Yeah, he was fantastic. But you say it's not the same now.
